blocks.prompt: 5 Prove that \(f(x) = \frac{\ln(2x)}{x^{2}}\) has local maximum at \(x = \frac{\sqrt{e}}{2}\).
blocks.explanation:
A proof with the Second Derivative Test.
Given \(f(x) = \frac{\ln(2x)}{x^{2}}\), defined for \(x > 0\).
Plan: quotient rule for \(f'\), show \(f'\left(\frac{\sqrt{e}}{2}\right) = 0\), then show \(f''\left(\frac{\sqrt{e}}{2}\right) < 0\).
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = \frac{\ln(2x)}{x^{2}}\), \(x > 0\).
To prove: \(f\) has a local maximum at \(x = \frac{\sqrt{e}}{2}\).
Method: Second Derivative Test: \(f'(c) = 0\) and \(f''(c) < 0\) give a relative maximum.

First derivative
\[f'(x) = \dfrac{x^{2} \cdot \frac{1}{x} - \ln(2x) \cdot 2x}{x^{4}}\]
\[= \dfrac{x - 2x\ln(2x)}{x^{4}}\]
\[= \dfrac{1 - 2\ln(2x)}{x^{3}}\]
Why: quotient rule; \(\frac{d}{dx}\ln(2x) = \frac{2}{2x} = \frac{1}{x}\); then cancel one \(x\).

Stationary point
\[1 - 2\ln(2x) = 0\]
\[\ln(2x) = \tfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow 2x = e^{1/2}\]
\[x = \dfrac{\sqrt{e}}{2}\]
Why: \(x^{3} > 0\), so only the numerator can be zero; \(\ln u = k\) means \(u = e^{k}\).

Second derivative
Write \(f'(x) = \frac{u}{v}\) with \(u = 1 - 2\ln(2x)\), \(v = x^{3}\):
\[f''(x) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^{2}}\]
\[u' = -\dfrac{2}{x}\]
Why: quotient rule again. At \(x = \frac{\sqrt{e}}{2}\) we have \(u = 0\), so the term \(uv'\) vanishes.

Value of \(f''\) at the point
\[f''\left(\tfrac{\sqrt{e}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{u'}{v} = -\dfrac{2}{x^{4}}\]
\[x^{4} = \dfrac{e^{2}}{16}\]
\[f''\left(\tfrac{\sqrt{e}}{2}\right) = -\dfrac{32}{e^{2}} < 0\]
Why: \(\frac{u'v}{v^{2}} = \frac{u'}{v} = \frac{-2/x}{x^{3}}\); and \(\left(\frac{\sqrt{e}}{2}\right)^{4} = \frac{e^{2}}{16}\).

Conclusion
\(f'\left(\frac{\sqrt{e}}{2}\right) = 0\) and \(f''\left(\frac{\sqrt{e}}{2}\right) < 0\), so \(f\) has a local maximum at \(x = \frac{\sqrt{e}}{2}\).
\[f\left(\tfrac{\sqrt{e}}{2}\right) = \dfrac{\ln\sqrt{e}}{e/4} = \dfrac{1/2}{e/4} = \dfrac{2}{e}\]
Why: Second Derivative Test; the value is extra information.
Check: \(\frac{\sqrt{e}}{2} \approx 0.824\). \(f'(0.7) > 0\) since \(\ln 1.4 \approx 0.34 < 0.5\), and \(f'(1) < 0\) since \(\ln 2 \approx 0.69 > 0.5\): the sign changes from \(+\) to \(-\).
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: \(f'\left(\frac{\sqrt{e}}{2}\right) = 0\) and \(f''\left(\frac{\sqrt{e}}{2}\right) = -\frac{32}{e^{2}} < 0\), so \(f\) has a local maximum at \(x = \frac{\sqrt{e}}{2}\) (maximum value \(\frac{2}{e}\)).
